knowledge_point.title: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Sine

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int \frac{\frac{8}{5}}{\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First factor the constant in the denominator:

$$
\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}=\sqrt{4(1-(\frac{1}{4})x^{2})}
$$

Use the linear substitution $u=\frac{x}{2}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{1}{2},\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(2)\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

Apply the basic inverse-trigonometric integral:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \int \frac{\frac{8}{5}}{\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= \frac{4}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(\frac{x}{2})^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= \frac{4}{5}(2)\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{8}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{8 \operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}}{5}+C \\  &= \frac{8 \operatorname{arcsin}{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)}}{5}+C\end{aligned}
$$
